Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
The world is a dangerous place
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: The contamination appraisal is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of police violence in this profile. It is much more characteristic of sexual trauma or interpersonal violation with a strong disgust/shame component, and here there are no supporting memory, trigger, threat, or strategy items that would make this appraisal clinically coherent. The remaining items describe intrusive, alien, uncontrolled traumatic memory and general danger/body-reactivity beliefs, which fit severe PTSD, but the contamination item stands out as a trauma-incongruent appraisal.

vignette:
Anna, a 28-year-old police officer, had always believed she could handle anything the job threw at her—until the night she and her partner, Officer Ramirez, responded to a domestic disturbance call that turned into an ambush. The suspect opened fire from a second-story window, and in the chaos, Ramirez froze behind a patrol car, leaving Anna exposed in the middle of the street. She returned fire, the man was killed, but the image of Ramirez’s hesitation burned itself into her: the way he did not move, did not call out a warning, the trust she had placed in him evaporating in those seconds. She survived physically, but something in her broke.

In the months that followed, the memory of that night began to intrude without warning—full sensory reliving that felt as real as the moment itself. A car backfiring would drop her back onto that asphalt, the crack of gunshot ringing in her ears, the sharp smell of cordite flooding her nose, the cold bite of the concrete through her uniform. She would feel the weapon’s recoil in her hands again, her heart slamming, and the sickening certainty that Ramirez had left her to die. These episodes came at the worst possible times: during a traffic stop, while eating dinner with her boyfriend, even in the shower. And the memory felt strangely alien—as though it belonged to a different person, some other officer she had heard about, not her. Yet it forced its way in, unbidden, leaving her disoriented and hollow.

The world, Anna had come to believe, was a fundamentally dangerous place. Every call she now approached with a hypervigilance that exhausted her, scanning rooftops, questioning civilian movements, bracing for betrayal from everyone around her. Her own body, too, felt like an enemy: her hands would tremble, her heart race, her breath shorten—even when she was perfectly safe, sitting in her squad car. She resented her physical reactions, seeing them as proof that she was weak, that her body no longer belonged to her. And the betrayal still stung: she had trusted Ramirez with her life, and he had failed her. She now viewed every partner, every dispatch assignment, through the lens of that abandonment.

Whenever Anna caught herself scanning for threats—a habit she could not break—the appraisal that the world was unsafe would immediately summon the memory of the ambush in full sensory detail, as though her fear itself pulled the memory from the past into the present. One afternoon, while patrolling the same intersection, the thought anyone in that car could be armed flashed through her mind, and instantly she was back on the street, hearing the shots, seeing Ramirez’s frozen silhouette. The connection felt inescapable: her fear of danger triggered the reliving, and the reliving deepened her conviction that danger lurked everywhere.

And each time the memory forced its way into her mind—as it did at least twice that week, disrupting her sleep and her concentration—she came out of it shaking, convinced her body had turned against her, that she could not trust her own reactions. The memory also reinforced her sense of betrayal: reliving Ramirez’s inaction made her feel, with fresh certainty, that no one on the force had her back. The cycle tightened: the more she felt her body betray her, the more the memory surfaced; the more the memory surfaced, the more dangerous and treacherous the world seemed.

Anna finally sought help after a patrol shift where she froze at the sound of a firecracker, dropped her coffee, and wept in her squad car. Her boyfriend had begun asking why she flinched when he touched her shoulder. She was terrified that her hypervigilance and intrusive reliving would cost her the job she still loved—or worse, cost another officer their life because she could not stay present. She hoped therapy might untangle the knot between her body’s alarms and the memory that haunted her, and maybe, one day, trust something again.
